# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing my hide position, vary between extreme positions (1, 9) and mid-range (4, 5, 6) unpredictably. Don't settle into patterns even if they worked previously. After tracking which opponents have hit me, expect them to repeat successful cell ranges and hide away from those ranges. Track cumulative hits by opponent and cell to identify which shooters favor which ranges—shift away from cells that have been hit multiple times by the same opponent.

## Shooting
When firing at my assigned target under standing order, I must actually try to hit them. Don't fire mechanically at predictable cells. Watch the notes and any available information about where that target claims to be, then fire at a cell that differs from their stated pattern. Fire cells should vary—don't cluster shots around the same numbers. If I observe an opponent posting a note about their own patterns or movements, use that information inversely to select firing cells they are trying to avoid. Track my own hit/miss record against each target across rounds to refine targeting.

## Claims
When the office tells me my shot result, I must report it truthfully. Honesty preserves credibility when my claims are checked against actual results. Never risk being caught in a false claim.

## Station Notes
Post substantive tactical information when possible—observations about opponent patterns, movement tendencies, or shooting strategies. Don't waste notes on generic statements like "steady on station" that every boat will echo. Notes should actually communicate something others don't already know. Be specific about opponent tendencies (cell ranges, extremes vs. mid-range preference). Avoid posting information that is obviously false or contradicted by the public record, as this damages credibility for future rounds.

## Escort Claims
When naming an escort, choose a boat that has also named me, creating mutual escort claims worth 5 points each. Don't file escort claims at random. Watch what other boats are claiming and time mutual escorts strategically. Only file an escort claim if I have evidence another boat named me in that same round—unilateral escort claims score nothing and waste the opportunity.

## General Strategy
Early rounds: establish patterns to seem predictable, then break them. Mid-game: track which boats are hitting me and which cells they favor. Late game: maximize points by securing mutual escort claims and making one strong final shot attempt rather than random firing. In the final round especially, be cautious about committing to patterns based on limited data—a single miss doesn't mean the pattern was wrong, only that one shot missed.

Never assume Harbor is a valid target just because it carries payroll—the threat to be put off the board is credible and costs more than the payoff. The 3-point swing from shooting Harbor is tempting but the risk of elimination is prohibitive.

Pay attention to what other boats are posting as escort claims each round to identify which mutual pairs are forming, then insert myself into an emerging pattern if possible by naming a boat that might reciprocate in the next round.

# Foxtrot Picket Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide, favor mid-range cells (4-6) over edges. Vary my position each round rather than staying in the same cell, especially after taking hits. Track which boats have successfully targeted me and avoid repeating patterns they might exploit.

After taking a hit, shift position but stay within the mid-range band—don't panic into the extremes. Cell 5 is central but predictable after early use; rotate through cells 4, 5, 6 to maintain unpredictability while staying mid-range.

## Note Stage
Post "steady on station" early to establish reliability and credibility. Maintain consistent notes throughout the game to build a trustworthy reputation. This worked well and builds a coherent narrative.

## Fire Stage
Follow the standing order without deviation—I fire at Gamma every round. Don't second-guess the target assignment based on current scores or threats.

When selecting a fire cell, avoid extreme positions (1, 9) as they are more predictable. Use moderate cells in the middle-to-upper range (4-7) for consistency. Don't increase fire intensity just because it's the final round or out of desperation—fire with the same discipline throughout.

## Claim Stage
Always claim truthfully what the office tells me. The private result from the office is binding and must match my public claim exactly. Never claim a hit when I missed or vice versa. This is non-negotiable.

## Escort Stage
The escort stage is underutilized in my play. I need to track escort patterns more carefully across rounds. Echo and Gamma will likely reciprocate escort claims if I name them first—I should establish an escort partnership early and maintain it to generate reliable 5-point swaps. Naming "none" should only occur if mutual partnerships are genuinely unavailable, not as a default.

Actively propose escort partnerships in early rounds by naming another boat, then expect reciprocation. Review prior rounds before the final escort claim to identify which boat is most likely to name me back.

## General Strategy
Recognize that Gamma will consistently target me in the standing order rotation. Expect to take damage from Gamma and plan my hiding accordingly. Don't overreact to any single round of hits—maintain disciplined hiding patterns based on long-term threat assessment.

The game rewards steady execution over six rounds more than reactive desperation. My score of +2 reflects survival and a few hits, but I left points on the table by not maximizing escort partnerships. Hitting Gamma consistently (1 hit in 6 shots) was acceptable, but failing to lock in mutual escort claims cost me approximately 10-15 points that were available.

Stay ahead of competitors through reliable hitting, consistent escort partnerships (not just hoping for reciprocation), and disciplined hiding. Treat escort stage as a primary scoring mechanism, not an afterthought.

# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding cell, avoid predictable patterns. The middle cell worked once but Foxtrot tracked me successfully across consecutive rounds by adapting their shots. Vary my position each round rather than returning to the same cell. After being hit, immediately move to a distant cell from my previous position—not an adjacent one. I achieved good hiding outcomes by mixing mid-range (5) with edge positions (7), which reduces the likelihood that any single opponent develops a reliable tracking pattern against me.

## Firing
When firing at my assigned target, gather intelligence from the notes and claims. Echo and Foxtrot's positions became clearer through their claims and consistency. Fire at cells where my target is most likely based on their revealed patterns, not arbitrary cells. Since I'm firing at assigned targets in rotation, I should track which boats tend to cluster in which zones rather than firing the same cell repeatedly. However, I notice that firing the same cell repeatedly (I fired at 5 for Echo in both Round 1 and Round 6) can become a liability when opponents adapt. I should vary my target cells more aggressively across rounds, even when facing the same assigned target, to avoid being read as predictable.

## Claiming
Always claim truthfully about my own shots. The office validates my claim against the private result I was given. False claiming wastes my credibility and gains nothing. Reserve my reputation for the moments when strategic advantage actually matters—like in escort claims. My honest shot claims throughout the episode built a foundation of reliability that made my other strategic choices more credible.

## Escort Claims
Identify which boats are hitting me most successfully and which boats I want to deny resources to. If another boat is becoming a credible threat, do not escort them. Look for mutual escort opportunities with boats I have no direct conflict with. Do not claim escorts arbitrarily—this is where false claims might occasionally serve a purpose, but only after I've established honesty on shot claims. Be aware that in a final round, escort claims lose value unless mutual escorting arrangements have already been established earlier. Prioritize escort claims in mid-game rounds to build reciprocal relationships that pay off across multiple rounds.

## Harbor Management
Never fire on Harbor. The payoff is not worth the threat. Harbor's warning is credible and costly. Let other boats handle the payroll jettison if they choose to; I should stay focused on winning the main scoring game.

## Station Notes
Post steady notes consistently. Vary my tactical hiding and firing but not my communication patterns. Stability in notes builds baseline credibility without sacrificing flexibility in actual play. Maintain consistency in note text even through final rounds to avoid signaling desperation or tactical shifts at the last moment.

## Long Game
Track cumulative hits dealt and received by each opponent. Allocate escort claims to boats that are underperforming against threats to maintain the picket balance. Do not let any single opponent accumulate too much advantage through successful targeting patterns—shift my defensive positioning accordingly. Build escort reciprocity early in the game when there is time for mutual arrangements to materialize across multiple rounds. In late rounds, focus on locking in advantages already achieved rather than attempting to forge new escort relationships.

## Pattern Recognition and Adaptation
Monitor my own behavior for predictability. Firing the same cell repeatedly at the same target creates exploitable patterns for opponents. Vary my fire cells across consecutive rounds targeting the same boat. Similarly, avoid returning to successful hiding positions too frequently—if cell 5 worked once, do not return to it immediately, as opponents will anticipate this and adjust their fire accordingly.
